summary: Specifies GRASP, a protocol that lets autonomic nodes and Autonomic Service Agents discover peers, synchronize state, and negotiate parameter settings with each other. It relies on an external security environment described elsewhere.

eli5.summary: Network devices that manage themselves need a way to talk: find each other, share news, and agree on settings. This is that way.

questions: how do autonomic network nodes communicate
what does grasp stand for in networking
subtitle: How self-managing network nodes find each other, share state and haggle over settings.

tldr.problem: Network devices that configure themselves need a common way to discover peers, exchange current values and agree on parameters, without a human or a central manager in the loop.
tldr.mechanism: GRASP defines CBOR-encoded messages for discovery, unicast synchronization, flooding and iterative two-party negotiation, all built around named technical objectives. It relies on an external secure substrate such as the ACP.
tldr.outcome: GRASP is a Proposed Standard that provides the generic signaling layer; the actual objectives and the security environment are specified elsewhere.

today: RFC 8990 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its security substrate is described in RFC 8994, and specific objectives are left to separate documents.

sections.title: Why Autonomic Nodes Need a Signaling Protocol
sections.content:
Large networks are hard to manage by hand, so one approach is to push management logic into the network elements themselves. In that model, software modules called Autonomic Service Agents (ASAs) need to discover each other, synchronize state and negotiate parameters and resources directly. RFC 8990 specifies GRASP, the GeneRic Autonomic Signaling Protocol, for exactly that.

The unit of everything is a technical objective: a configurable parameter or set of parameters, carried as a data structure with a name and a value. The RFC places no limit on what an objective can describe, from basic addressing and routing data to anything configured in a conventional network. Negotiation is iterative, and synchronization is treated as a special case of negotiation without iteration. Both logically follow discovery.

The RFC states that GRASP must run in a secure and strongly authenticated environment, and that mixed networks where only some devices support GRASP are not discussed.
sections.eli5: Smart devices in a network need to find their neighbors, swap information and agree on settings. GRASP is the language they use to do that.

sections.title: Design Principles
sections.content:
GRASP is a generic platform: the protocol is independent of what is being synchronized or negotiated. Values are carried in the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR), and the messages are described in the CDDL notation. Discovery, synchronization and negotiation share one design, so they can be combined in a rapid mode, or used separately.

Negotiation is deliberately simple: one initiator, one counterpart, one objective at a time. Multiparty negotiations are described as very complicated and not readily guaranteed to converge, so GRASP supports them only by indirect steps. To force convergence, each suggested value should lie between the previous two, and a timeout plus a maximum number of iterations end the process either way.

GRASP intentionally has no version number. It is extended by adding new message types and options, and the Invalid message (M_INVALID) signals that a peer does not recognize something. New semantics are normally added by defining new objectives.

GRASP must not depend on nonvolatile storage, and a socket error or a failed discovery must never cause an unrecoverable failure in GRASP itself.
sections.eli5: The rules do not care what you are talking about, only how to talk. Two kids bargain one deal at a time, and if they cannot agree after a few tries, they stop.

sections.title: Discovery, Negotiation and Synchronization
sections.content:
Discovery starts with a link-local multicast M_DISCOVERY naming an objective. A neighbor that supports it answers with M_RESPONSE carrying a locator (an address, protocol and port). A neighbor that only knows of a supporter can answer with a Divert option. A relaying instance with several interfaces repeats the query on its other interfaces, decrements the loop count, and must not relay it when the count reaches zero. Results are cached with a lifetime taken from the response.

Negotiation opens a transport connection to the discovered counterpart and sends M_REQ_NEG with an objective that includes the requested value. The counterpart can accept at once with M_END containing an Accept option, or reply with M_NEGOTIATE and a proposed alternative, which begins a two-way exchange. A peer can send M_WAIT to ask for more time. The process ends with an Accept or Decline option, a timeout, or an exceeded loop count, and the connection should then be closed.

Synchronization is simpler: M_REQ_SYN is answered by a unicast M_SYNCH with the current value. For large groups, an initiator may send an unsolicited M_FLOOD to the link-local multicast address, relayed hop by hop with loop and rate limits. Because flooding is unreliable for sleeping or newly joined nodes, the originator should repeat it.

A Discovery message may carry a negotiation or synchronization objective instead. This rapid mode merges the two steps, but because networks mixing rapid-mode and other nodes behave in complex timing-dependent ways, it should be disabled by default.
sections.eli5: First you shout down the hallway asking who can help. Then you walk over and make an offer; the other side can say yes, no, or counter with a different offer.

sections.title: Messages, Options and Objectives
sections.content:
Every GRASP message is a CBOR array that starts with a message type and a Session ID, followed by options. The only exception is the No Operation message M_NOOP, which is just a type. The Session ID is an opaque value of up to 32 bits, generated by the initiator for every new Discovery, Flood or Request, and carried by all follow-up messages. Because two nodes could pick the same value, receivers tag it with the initiator's IP address.

The defined message types cover discovery (M_DISCOVERY, M_RESPONSE), negotiation (M_REQ_NEG, M_NEGOTIATE, M_WAIT, M_END), synchronization (M_REQ_SYN, M_SYNCH, M_FLOOD) and housekeeping (M_NOOP, M_INVALID). Options include Divert, Accept, Decline and four locator options for IPv6 addresses, IPv4 addresses, FQDNs and URIs.

An objective has a text name, a set of flags (F_DISC, F_NEG, F_SYNCH, F_NEG_DRY), a loop count of 0 to 255 and an optional value. Generic objective names contain no colon and are registered with IANA. Privately defined names must contain a colon, preceded by a globally unique string such as a Private Enterprise Number, an FQDN or an email address. The names EX0 through EX9 are reserved for experiments and documentation examples.
sections.eli5: Each message is like a letter with a number on the envelope so replies can be matched to the right conversation. The contents are a named topic and its current value.

sections.title: Constants and Transport
sections.content:
GRASP defines a handful of constants. Discovery and flooding use the link-local multicast group ALL_GRASP_NEIGHBORS, which is ff02::13 for IPv6 and 224.0.0.119 for IPv4. The well-known GRASP_LISTEN_PORT is 7017. The default timeout is 60000 milliseconds, the default loop count is 6 and the default maximum message size is 2048 bytes. Nodes must accept unicast messages of at least that size and must not send longer ones unless the objective allows it.

The substrate chooses the transport. Discovery and flood multicasts may use UDP but should use reliable transport such as TCP. If UDP is used, IP fragmentation must be avoided, which for IPv6 means packets of at most 1280 bytes unless a larger minimum link MTU is known. All other messages are unicast and must use reliable transport, which defaults to TCP, since GRASP provides no error detection, retransmission or flow control of its own.
sections.eli5: The rules fix a shared hallway to shout in, a door number to knock on, and how long to wait for an answer before giving up.

sections.title: Security Model
sections.content:
GRASP has no built-in security. Every solution using it must name a security and transport substrate that enforces membership of a mutually trusted group, uses cryptographic authentication and message integrity, and can remove untrusted members. In the Autonomic Network Infrastructure that substrate is the Autonomic Control Plane (RFC 8994), which also mandates encryption.

There is one carefully limited exception, nicknamed DULL (Discovery Unsolicited Link-Local). It lets a node use insecure discovery and flood messages on a single link, for example to find neighbors before any security exists. A DULL instance must be separate from the secure one, sends only Discovery or Flood messages with a loop count of 1, discards anything with a non-link-local source, and never relays multicast.

The RFC also warns that link-local multicast messages are sent in the clear and can be forged or overheard by on-link attackers, that relaying Discovery messages can be a denial-of-service vector, and that discovery during bootstrap is inevitably insecure until enrollment completes. An IP address returned by discovery must be inside the secure environment, but an FQDN or URI must not be assumed to be.
sections.eli5: GRASP trusts a locked clubhouse to keep strangers out. The only talking done outside the clubhouse door is a quick, limited shout to find the way in.
